title: Arista Lines Up Networking For 10 Gigawatts Of AI Systems
author: Timothy Prickett Morgan
text:
CONNECT

Arista Lines Up Networking For 10 Gigawatts Of AI Systems

Timothy Prickett Morgan

Timothy Prickett
Morgan

Co-Editor, Co-Founder, The Next Platform

Published
thu 5 Nov 2026 // 17:30 UTC

It takes a while to tame a new computing architecture, and so it is understandable that the AI-related ramp at all Ethernet switch makers – and particularly at arch rivals Cisco Systems and Arista Networks – has taken many years to come to fruition. And, to be frank, they are all just getting started.It is not just a matter of making higher bandwidth Ethernet switches and riding down the cost per bit flitted curves as the aggregate bandwidth per ASIC doubles and the cost of moving bits goes down a little, allowing for elastic consumption and larger and larger networks to balance out larger and larger clusters. That would be relatively easy, and pretty much defines the cloud networking era from 2010 through 2020.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

AI is different. It demands high radix devices and flatter networks because the workload is inherently latency sensitive, and given the extremely high cost of a GPU or XPU relative to other kinds of compute, keeping these compute engines waiting is economically devastating. If GPUs and XPUs were “cheap as chips,” an English phrase referring to the friend potatoes that accompany fried fish in pub food, we would tolerate some inefficiencies and interleave workloads across more devices and make it up in volume. That is not an option when it comes to AI training or AI inference – hasn’t been for years and won’t ever be again. The tokenomics will kill the goose that lays the golden trillions of tokens otherwise.Moreover, AI requires AI. To balance workloads across tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of accelerators in a datacenter or region and across millions of accelerators across regions requires all kinds of dynamic routing and switching and the processing of untold amounts of telemetry. Keeping these accelerators business means embedding AI into management tools, like Arista’s Autonomous Virtual Assistant, because human beings cannot correlate and analyze data at the pace of computers. Securing this infrastructure also requires AI because bad actors are also using AI to find vulnerabilities and exploit them. All of this development has also taken time.The Inevitability Of EthernetNo one – not hyperscalers, not cloud builders, not AI model builders, not national HPC labs, not sovereigns, not AMD – except Nvidia wants proprietary networks anywhere in the interconnect hierarchy for AI clusters. And Nvidia got out way ahead of everyone else in creating tightly coupled, shared memory GPU clusters and deserves its first mover advantages when it comes to market share, revenue, and profits. But, as I have pointed out, NVSwitch and NVLink are the InfiniBand of scale up and scale in networking and they will have to compete against more open – and presumably cheaper – alternatives based on Ethernet running ESUN or UALink protocols and perhaps native UALink for gluing GPU memories together and UCI-Express for gluing components together within an accelerator package.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

But this transition is going to take time. At the moment, Arista Networks is making money selling Ethernet switches for regular cloudy infrastructure and for AI front ends – the networks that connect AI clusters to the outside world and storage. The company is also making serious money peddling its R series Ethernet switches that are augmented with routing functions to do scale across datacenter linkages, which is used to make AI clusters span multiple datacenters and regions. This is necessary because you can only build a datacenter or region so big because power is often limited in a given geographic area. The hyperscalers and cloud builders have to spread it around.Arista has yet to make any serious money selling Ethernet switchery for scale up networks (also called the AI back end by some), but there are some trials that have been under way at the hyperscalers and cloud builders to run the ESUN and UALink over Ethernet (UALoE) protocols atop Ethernet fabrics.On a call with Wall Street analysts going over the company’s third quarter financial results, Jayshree Ullal, Arista’s chief executive officer, said that the company has worked with AMD, Arm, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and Qualcomm on rackscale switching based on its Etherlink switching and routing lines, and added that she expected for scale up trails based on the ESUN protocol to start in 2027, initially with rackscale systems with a radix of 128 or 144 accelerators within a rack and with as many as 1,000 accelerators across a row. (The number is almost certainly 1,024 accelerators, not 1,000, and she was speaking generally.) Production rollouts for ESUN scale up networks are not expected until 2028.This seems like a long time away, and the wonder is what is taking so long.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

Arista has not said it will embrace UALink switching, which will more directly competes against Nvidia’s NVSwitch stack, but that is always a possibility given the availability of third party UALink ASICs from Astera Labs, Marvell, Upscale AI, and maybe Panmnesia.Arista does not really have a play for scale in networking down on AI accelerator packages. That is something for AMD, Nvidia, Broadcom, Marvell, Alchip, and maybe Intel and Qualcomm to do.Before scale up ramps, there is plenty of money to be made peddling scale across and scale out networking for now, as Arista’s third quarter results show.

You can finally see the beginning of the proverbial hockey stick curve driven by GenAI in the product revenue curve shown above. Arista has been waiting years for that to happen.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

In the September quarter, Arista posted product sales of $3.19 billion, up 66.9 percent year on year and up 22.4 percent sequentially. Services revenues plug along behind that, as always, and grew by 17.9 percent to $467.6 million in the quarter.

Add it up, and total revenues for Q3 came to $3.66 billion, up 58.5 percent, and sequential growth was 20.5 percent overall. This is 2X to 3X higher sequential growth than is normal and is the highest level set by the company since its founding years. (Which almost don’t count because there are so few deals and so little money comparatively back in the beginning of a company.)Arista’s operating income was $1.64 billion, up 67.9 percent, and its net income was $1.56 billion, up 82.9 percent. That net income is a very healthy 42.7 percent of revenues, and it is the highest level of profits the company has ever enjoyed. The company exited Q3 with $14.36 billion in cash and equivalents and had $11.4 billion in customer purchase commitments and $6.84 billion in deferred revenues, also very healthy relative to the size of the business.Ullal gave us some numbers that allow us to update our annual Arista product segment model, which is shown below forecasting 2026 and 2027:

And here is the same data shown graphically so you can feel the curves:

On the call, Ullal said that Arista was on track to sell about $3.5 billion in AI front end and back end networking gear and services in 2026 and that this would double to $7 billion or so in 2027. Campus switching, which is an easy adjacency that helps take money away from Cisco and others, would hit $1.25 billion this year and grow to $2 billion next year. At the midpoint of growth targets, Arista will grow overall revenues by 52 percent in 2026 to hit $13.3 billion and will grow by another 39.1 percent in 2027 to reach $18.5 billion.We have to guess how the non-AI and campus portions of the Arista business will do, and gave it our best shot in the table and chart above. The portions of the business not relating to AI front end and back end networks (which does include scale across networking linking datacenters and regions) are growing well in 2026, mostly thanks to that scale across gear that is in the routing product segment. The core cloud and datacenter switching business and the edge segment are growing, but not by much. I see this dichotomy in servers, too. Traditional workloads are growing more in servers, in fact, than they are in switching. This could yet change.

Also looking ahead, Ullal said that its current customers that account for 10 percent or more of annual revenue – that would be Microsoft and Meta Platforms – are working with Arista on ESUN scale up networks for their respective Maia and MTIA XPUs and are still on track to be big spenders in 2026 and 2027. She added that the company might add one or perhaps two more big spenders in the coming year, which is fueling its growth in 2027 presumably.The market is inflecting, hard. In 2024 and 2025, said Ullal, Arista was talking about having four or five customers with AI clusters in the range of 50,000 to 100,000 Nvidia GPUs, and seeing a lot of InfiniBand still going into machines. Here in 2026, Arista already has more than a hundred customers using its AI-centric Etherlink switches, and by the end of 2027, she is forecasting that the company will provide networking for 10 gigawatts of AI cluster capacity and will be linking ten or more different kinds of accelerators.
